original_summary: Dudo (Perudo) is a bluffing dice game for 2 to 10 players. Each player rolls hidden dice, players take turns bidding ever-higher claims about how many dice of a face are on the table (ones are wild), and a challenge ('Dudo') reveals the dice and costs the wrong party a die. The last player with dice wins.

review.evidence: Every simple policy loses. Always calling Dudo loses about half the time against honest openings near T/3, which is the expected count of a face once ones count as wild. Always raising runs into an impossible bid that gets called. The starting seat changes each round because the loser opens.
Each roll is random, but over many rounds the better player wins by judging probability from their own dice and reading what opponents' bids imply. The ace-conversion rules add skilled edge cases.
Beginners can play to the expected count. Experts track bidding patterns, bluff deliberately and adjust as dice counts shrink. The game is not solved for several players.
The core of the game is hidden dice. Players infer opponents' hands from their bids and choose between bluffing and challenging.
A challenge is settled by counting the revealed dice. Elimination and the winner follow by arithmetic.

Bidding is open-ended, so the number of choice steps per round is unbounded. The ace halving and doubling rules add rule chains. Ten players with five dice each is long and exceeds the attribute limits. Play is turn-based and text-only, which suits the platform.

problems: Unbounded bidding chains exceed the limit of 4 choice steps per round.
The ace conversion rules (halve or more than double) add complexity without adding much reasoning at small scale.
Up to 10 players with 5 dice each exceeds the attribute and step budgets, and games can run very long.
Previous variation: a separate random draw to pick the first opener put hand 1 at two random draws, over the limit of 1.
Previous variation: it did not say that the dice roll is a single deal operation, so the roll looked like many independent draws, and it did not say that N is a single count.
Previous variation: with T=2 the opening bound floor(T/3)=0 allowed a Q=0 bid. Such a bid is always true, so it is not a claim, and Dudo against it always loses.

changes.what: Each round has at most 4 choice steps: an opening bid, up to two responses that can raise by +1 or +2, and a final forced Dudo or Calza.
changes.why: Keeps the round within 4 choice steps while keeping the escalation of bids and the bluff-or-call tension.
changes.fixes: Unbounded bidding chains exceed the limit of 4 choice steps per round.

changes.what: Ones are always wild, and bids may only name faces 2 to 6. There is no switching to aces.
changes.why: Removes a special-case rule chain, while the wild ones still make counting interesting.
changes.fixes: The ace conversion rules (halve or more than double) add complexity without adding much reasoning at small scale.

changes.what: 2 to 4 players with 5 dice each, and a cap of 30 rounds after which the player with the most dice wins.
changes.why: Keeps the hidden state within 20 dice and the game short enough to play.
changes.fixes: Up to 10 players with 5 dice each exceeds the attribute and step budgets, and games can run very long.

changes.what: The separate first-opener draw is removed. Seat 1 opens round 1, and afterwards the loser opens as in the original.
changes.why: Every round, including round 1, then has exactly one random event: the roll. A one-time opening advantage is negligible over many rounds.
changes.fixes: Previous variation: a separate random draw to pick the first opener put hand 1 at two random draws, over the limit of 1.

changes.what: The rules state that each round's roll is one deal operation that produces every player's hidden dice at once, and that N is computed by one count operation over all revealed dice.
changes.why: Makes random_draws_per_round = 1 true by construction and keeps the step count fixed.
changes.fixes: Previous variation: it did not say that the dice roll is a single deal operation, so the roll looked like many independent draws, and it did not say that N is a single count.

changes.what: The opening quantity bound becomes max(1, floor(T/3)) <= Q <= ceil(T/2).
changes.why: Every legal bid is now a real claim of at least one die. At T=2 the only opening quantity is Q=1.
changes.fixes: Previous variation: with T=2 the opening bound floor(T/3)=0 allowed a Q=0 bid. Such a bid is always true, so it is not a claim, and Dudo against it always loses.

keeps: Hidden dice, with each player seeing only their own.
Bids are claims about the whole table, and ones are wild.
Bids must escalate, and players choose between raising and calling Dudo.
The Calza (exact) call, which can win a die back.
Losing a die for being wrong, elimination at zero dice, the loser opening the next round, and the last player with dice winning.

recommendation.reason: The hidden-dice bluffing core is ideal for inference and opponent modelling. The revised short structure fits every platform limit with exactly one random draw per round.

variation.name: Short Dudo
variation.summary: A compact Dudo for 2 to 4 players. Each round has a single hidden roll, an opening bid, up to two escalating raises, and a forced Dudo or Calza at the end. Losing all your dice eliminates you. The last player with dice, or the player with the most dice after 30 rounds, wins.
variation.rules:
SETUP. 2 to 4 players sit in a fixed seat order: seat 1, seat 2, and so on. Each player starts with 5 dice. Seat 1 is the opener for round 1. There is no random draw before play.

EACH ROUND.
1. ROLL. In one deal operation, every player still in the game receives a fresh random roll of as many six-sided dice as they currently hold. This single operation produces all hands at once and is the only random event of the round. Each player is shown only their own dice. T is the total number of dice still in play, and every player is told T and every player's dice count.
2. OPENING BID (choice 1). The opener chooses a face from 2 to 6 and a quantity Q with max(1, floor(T/3)) <= Q <= ceil(T/2). The bid means 'at least Q dice among all players show this face, with every 1 counting as this face'. The bid is announced to all.
3. RESPONSE 1 (choice 2). The next player in seat order who is still in the game chooses one of four options:
   (a) Raise +1: the new quantity is the current quantity + 1, with any face from 2 to 6 the player chooses.
   (b) Raise +2: the new quantity is the current quantity + 2, with any face from 2 to 6 the player chooses.
   (c) Dudo: challenge the current bid as false.
   (d) Calza: claim the count is exactly the current quantity.
   A raise is illegal if the new quantity would exceed T. If both raises are illegal, only Dudo or Calza may be chosen. The choice is announced. A player who raises becomes the current bidder.
4. RESPONSE 2 (choice 3). This step happens only if response 1 was a raise. The next player in seat order who is still in the game makes the same kind of choice against the current bid. With 2 players, this is the opener again.
5. FINAL RESPONSE (choice 4). This step happens only if response 2 was a raise. The next player in seat order who is still in the game must choose Dudo or Calza. Raising is not allowed.
6. REVEAL. All dice are shown. N is the number of dice showing the current bid face plus the number showing 1, computed as one count over all dice.
7. SETTLE. If the call was Dudo: when N >= the current quantity, the caller loses 1 die; otherwise the current bidder loses 1 die. If the call was Calza: when N equals the current quantity exactly, the caller gains 1 die, up to a maximum of 5; otherwise the caller loses 1 die.
8. ELIMINATION. A player with 0 dice is out and is skipped in seat order from then on.
9. NEXT OPENER. The player who lost a die opens the next round. After a successful Calza, the caller opens. If that player was eliminated, the next player in seat order who is still in the game opens.
10. END CHECK. If only one player remains, the game ends. If 30 rounds have been played, the game ends. Otherwise a new round begins.

There is no talk phase. Bids and calls are the only communication.
variation.objective: If only one player has dice left, that player wins. If 30 rounds are completed with two or more players still in, the player holding the most dice wins. If two or more players tie for the most dice, the game is a draw.
variation.expected_effect: Players must judge the likely count from their own dice and the expected one-third of the other dice, then read each raise as evidence about the bidder's hand. Bluffs that are too large get called, and calls made too eagerly lose against honest bids near T/3. Always calling Dudo, always raising and always calling Calza all lose to sensible play. The new opening floor guarantees every bid is a real claim, and each round has exactly one random event. Talk is left out: bids already carry the signalling, and there is no shared plan anyone could propose that others would gain by following.

balanced.evidence: Main decision, 2 players at the start (T=10, own 5 dice). The opener must bid Q between floor(10/3)=3 and ceil(10/2)=5. Each unseen die shows a given face or a 1 with probability 1/3. If the opener bids Q=3 on their best face with own count c, the chance the bid is true is: c>=3: 1.00; c=2: 1-(2/3)^5 = 0.87; c=1: 1-0.132-0.329 = 0.54. The best face of 5 dice, counting ones, is usually 2-3, so a minimum opening is true about 85-90% of the time. Policy table (approximate). Always Dudo as responder: wins about 10-15% of hands against a sensible opener, so it loses. Always Calza: needs N=Q exactly, about 0.33 at best (c=2: 5*(1/3)*(2/3)^4 = 0.329), so it wins about 25-33% of hands and loses. Always Raise +2: from 3 to 5 on own best face (own count about 2.7) needs about 2.3 more from 5 unseen dice, whose mean is 1.67. That is true about 45% of the time, and the opener can Dudo it or re-raise to force a call, so it loses. Always raise when legal: in 2 players the opener holds response 2, so the raiser becomes the forced final caller and is exposed to a bluffed re-raise; this is no better than always Dudo. Always open at the maximum Q=5: true only about 20-45%, while the minimum opening is about 85%, so it is worse. No option is strictly better whatever the opponent does: Dudo is good exactly when the bid is false, raising is good when it is true, and that truth is hidden. No thoughtless policy avoids losing. Seat edge: the opener has a per-hand edge (about 60-70%), but the loser of the previous hand opens, so the edge works as a catch-up rather than a fixed seat advantage. The first opener only matters for hand 1. Both players can realistically win. In 2 players each hand removes one die unless a Calza succeeds. With 10 dice in total, someone is eliminated within about 9 losses, so the 30-hand cap and its draw rule rarely apply. There is no labelled payoff ordering to misstate.

playable.evidence: 1) Random draws. The limit is random_draws_per_round <= 1. Hand 1 has two draws: the setup draw that picks the first opener, and the dice roll. Every hand also rolls up to 20 independent dice. That stays within the limit only if the whole roll is one deal operation producing all hands; the design does not say so, and the stated '1 draw' leaves out the setup draw. 2) Degenerate legal bid. With T=2 (1 die each), floor(2/3)=0, so Q=0 is a legal opening. 'At least 0 dice show the face' is always true, so the bid is not a claim and Dudo against it always loses. The rules should not allow a trivially true bid. Everything else is fine. Hidden elements: one per-player hidden hand. Attributes: about 14 (4 hands as lists, 4 dice counts, T, Q, face, current bidder, opener, call type, N, hand counter), within 20. Choice steps: 4. Steps: 14, plausible, though counting N across up to 20 dice must be one count operation or the step budget is at risk. The game is finite (elimination, or a cap of 30 hands) and decided by arithmetic on dice counts. Responses are sequential, and the order is the point, so that is fine. The 2-player order (opener, responder, opener, responder) and the 3-4 player order are both stated, and so is skipping eliminated players. Having no talk with 3-4 players is sensible: there is no joint proposal for anyone to follow, every bid is announced before the next choice, and bids already carry the signalling. There is no repeated cooperation dilemma to check.

reasoning_over_luck.evidence: The dice are hidden information, and every bid is a signal to infer from: a raise on face g suggests the raiser holds g or ones. A player sets Dudo, raise or Calza against a probability made from known own dice plus unknown dice at 1/3 each. Example: c=2 and Q=3 gives 0.87 true, so Dudo is wrong; a raise to Q=5 with own 2 and 5 unseen dice gives about 0.21 true, so Dudo is right. Players also bluff with the forced-call structure: a response-2 raise forces the next player to commit. Opponent modelling (how often does this player bluff a re-raise?) carries across hands. Chance: one hand's deal can decide that hand, but a game takes about 9 or more hands with a catch-up for the loser. I estimate about 35-45% of results are luck-driven. When both players play well, the winner comes from many probabilistic calls rather than one hidden draw. A player who reasons well (minimum honest openings, calling improbable bids, re-raising to force calls) clearly beats one who does not.

required_changes: Remove the separate first-opener draw. Derive the first opener from the hand-1 roll (e.g. the player with the highest dice sum opens; ties go to the earliest seat), or fix it as seat 1. Either way each hand has exactly one random draw.

State that each hand's roll is a single deal operation that produces every player's hidden hand at once, so that random_draws_per_round = 1 truly holds. State that N is computed by one count operation over all hands.
Change the opening bid bound to max(1, floor(T/3)) <= Q <= ceil(T/2), so that no trivially true Q=0 bid exists when T=2.

balanced.evidence:
Main decision, 2 players, T=10, both players at 5 dice. Each die matches a named face (that face or a 1) with p=1/3. Each player sees only their own 5 dice, so all that is unknown is the opponent's 5 dice. An opponent's 5 dice yield X matches, with X ~ Bin(5,1/3): P0=.132, P1=.329, P2=.329, P3=.165, P4=.041, P5=.004.

Opening bid (Q from 3 to 5). The opener names its best face, which typically gives k=2 or 3 own matches. P(true) at the minimum Q=3: k=1 gives .539, k=2 gives .868, k=3 gives 1.0. So a minimum opening on the best face is about 85-90% true.

Responder 1, holding j matches of the bid face:
| option | win probability (approx.) |
| Dudo | j=0: .46; j=1: .13; j=2: 0 (and lower once you account for what the opener's face choice reveals) |
| Calza | j=0: .165; j=1: .329; j=2: .329 (exactness rarely pays) |
| Raise +1 on own face with j' matches, bid of 4 | true with j'=2: .539; j'=3: .868 |

After a raise, the opener at response 2 knows its own count of the new face. It either Dudos with a well-informed estimate or raises on its own face (a bid of 5 with 3 own matches is true .539). The final responder then must call, but it knows its own half exactly. Every option wins in some states and loses in others, so none is strictly better.

Thoughtless policies under the WINNER RULE (a lost die is a step toward elimination):
- Always Dudo at response 1: loses about 85% of rounds against a minimum best-face opening. Against a random opener (random face and Q) it wins maybe 45-50%. It loses the game.
- Always Calza: loses about 67-83% of calls and is eliminated quickly.
- Always Raise +1 (the first option): a sensible opponent Dudos whenever the bid is unlikely. The raiser loses whenever it chose a face it does not hold. It loses against sensible play and is roughly even against random play.
- Always the highest legal raise (+2): this is the same as above but worse, since bids of 5 or more with few own matches are mostly false.
- Always bidding the minimum on the best face as opener: this is a strong opening, but responders can shift the risk by raising on their own faces with true bids. It does not guarantee a win.
No policy wins or draws almost always.

Seat and move order: in 2 players the opener never makes the forced call and the non-opener always has the last word. The opener's edge (a minimum opening that is about 88% true) roughly offsets the non-opener's edge of calling last with full knowledge of its own half. The opener is the previous round's loser, which is a mild catch-up effect.

With 3-4 players, a seat beyond the active chain is untouched that round. This edge is dynamic, because the losing player opens and action moves forward round by round, so no fixed seat is shielded.

Both players can realistically win. There are no labelled payoff orderings to check, and no cooperation structure that 'higher total wins' could break.

playable.evidence:
Rules are complete:
- The opening range max(1,floor(T/3)) to ceil(T/2) is non-empty for every T of 2 or more (T=2 gives [1,1]; T=3 gives [1,2]).
- Raise legality (new Q at most T) and the fallback to Dudo or Calza are specified.
- The final response forbids raising, so each round has at most 4 choices and always ends in a call.
- Settlement covers Dudo true and false, and Calza exact and not exact.
- The 5-die cap on a Calza gain is stated.
- The next opener is defined for every case: the loser, the successful Calza caller, or the next living seat if the loser was eliminated.
- Elimination skipping is defined.
- The end rule is last player standing or 30 rounds, then most dice, with ties a draw.

The game is finite (30-round cap) and decided by arithmetic on stored dice counts.

Limits:
| limit | stated | maximum |
| steps | 14 | 20 |
| choice steps | 4 | 4 |
| attributes | 14 | 20 |
| hidden elements | 1 (hands) | 3 |
| random draws per round | 1 | 1 |
| rounds | 30 | 40 |

The 14 attributes cover up to 4 dice counts, bid quantity, face, bidder, call type, caller, opener, T, N, round number and stage, which fits.

Engine features:
- 'Step happens only if response 1 was a raise' is a single-step `when` condition, not a conditional block.
- Hidden hands, sequential choice, elimination and variable player count are all supported.
- The roll is one deal operation, using the deck-draw workaround.
- N is one count over revealed hands.
No board, judge or clock is needed.

Talk with 3-4 players: omitting it is sensible. Bids already carry the information players reason about, so free talk would add words without a decision. Players are never left guessing blindly.

The repeated-game cooperation test does not apply, because there is no cooperative option.
